description: Our team aims to explore how geological and environmental locations on Earth can help us understand the Moon and Mars. By analyzing eleven terrestrial sites, we will compare their geological features, mineral composition, water resources, and surface conditions with those observed on both planetary bodies. Our goal is to identify valuable terrestrial analogues that could support future lunar base development and Martian exploration.
summary:
This project investigates how terrestrial environments can contribute to scientific research and future exploration of the Moon and Mars. It focuses on eleven locations across different parts of the world, analyzing their geological, mineralogical, geomorphological, and environmental characteristics. The investigation examines features such as volcanic formations, impact craters, ancient lake deposits, evaporite minerals, water resources, erosion, microbial communities, and subsurface structures.

By integrating scientific publications, satellite imagery, remote-sensing datasets, and observations from NASA planetary missions, the project will compare these terrestrial environments with documented features of the Moon and Mars. It will evaluate the relevance and limitations of each location as a partial planetary analogue, identifying which sites offer the strongest scientific comparisons for specific exploration objectives.

Ultimately, this research seeks to demonstrate how studying Earth's geological diversity can improve our understanding of planetary environments and contribute to preparing for permanent lunar bases and future human exploration of Mars.
details:
Our project works by evaluating eleven terrestrial locations around the world to determine how their geological and environmental characteristics can help us understand the Moon and Mars. We will analyze seven main aspects: geology and mineralogy, topography and environmental conditions, water resources, erosion and surface processes, microbiology and astrobiology, subsurface structures, and mobility and robotic exploration.

The investigation will use scientific publications, satellite imagery, remote-sensing datasets, and observations from NASA missions. Tools such as NASA Earthdata, NASA Worldview, ASTER GDEM, Landsat, Sentinel, and data from the Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter (LRO) and Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter (MRO) will support our comparisons.

The main benefit of this project is identifying terrestrial environments that can serve as partial analogues for specific lunar and Martian features. Its intended impact is to contribute to planetary research and provide scientific insights that may support future permanent lunar bases and human exploration of Mars.

The creative aspect of our project is connecting different geological environments across Earth with real challenges in space exploration. Instead of treating one location as a complete planetary equivalent, we evaluate how different places can contribute to understanding specific processes.

Our team considered scientific evidence, geological similarities, environmental conditions, available data, technological limitations, and the differences between Earth, the Moon, and Mars. These factors will help ensure that our conclusions are based on scientific comparisons rather than assumptions.
